title: Bilal on the roof
hook: the once-enslaved Bilal climbs the Ka'ba to call the adhan

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Haqq: the statues fell as he recited, truth has come, and falsehood vanished away. Did you clear one false thing from your room? Day two hundred eighty, the end of the week.

Who gets the best seat at the celebration? At most victory parties it's the generals, the donors, the old families. On the day Mecca opened, the early biographies say the Prophet ﷺ turned to one man and told him to climb up onto the roof of the Ka'ba and call the prayer. Not a chief of Quraysh. Not one of his own relatives. Bilal: a Black man from Abyssinian stock, born enslaved, in this very city. Some of the Meccan nobles standing below watched him go up, and the reports say a few of them muttered about it. Then his voice went out over the valley. Today, the man on the roof.
screen: `WHO GETS THE BEST SEAT?` → `CLIMB UP AND CALL.` → `BILAL, BORN ENSLAVED.`

segments.voice: To feel what that moment meant, go back to the early years in Mecca. Bilal was an early Muslim, and he belonged to a man named Umayya, one of the Prophet's fiercest enemies. The biographies say Umayya would drag him out into the midday heat of Mecca, lay him on the burning ground, and put a heavy rock on his chest, demanding he give up the one God. And Bilal would only say one word, over and over: ahad, ahad. One. One. Abu Bakr bought him and set him free. In Medina, Bilal's strong voice made him the first mu'adhdhin, the one who calls the adhan, five times a day. Now it's the conquest. The same streets. The same people, some of them. And the man they had crushed under a rock is standing on the roof of the Ka'ba, calling: God is greatest. The Qur'an puts the principle in one line, in Pickthall's translation: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct." Not the richest, not the best born. Bilal on the roof made that verse visible. Muslims still honor him; mosques and children carry his name, and the muezzin's role is often traced back to him. And this whole week has been one arc: a treaty that looked like losing, letters sealed and sent to kings, Safiyyah becoming a mother of believers, a head bowed on the camel, no blame on you today, truth has come. And, at the top of it, Bilal.
screen: `AHAD, AHAD — ONE, ONE.` · `THE FIRST MU'ADHDHIN.` · `THE NOBLEST IS THE BEST IN CONDUCT.` · `THIS WEEK: A VICTORY WITHOUT REVENGE.` · then, large: `BILAL ON TOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor someone once looked down on. Sit, and breathe slowly. Think of someone around you who usually gets overlooked. The quiet one on the team. The person who cleans the building. The relative who never gets asked for an opinion. Picture them for a moment in the place of honor, and ask yourself what one small thing you could do today to put them there: ask their advice, say their name with thanks, give them the good seat. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Bilal, the once-enslaved caller of the prayer, lifted to the top of the Ka'ba on the day Mecca opened.
Your line: bilal on top. Today, give the best seat, the first word or the credit to someone who doesn't usually get it. Day two hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Bilal as the first muezzin, and the adhan he called is still sung from mosques five times a day; his story is often told to teach that nobility lies in conduct, not birth.

original.note: Arabic: the one who calls the adhan, the call to prayer. Bilal was the first.

trapdoor: what you thought: a man with a good voice got a job.
what it means: the tortured, once-enslaved Bilal lifted above the nobles, the verse about nobility made visible.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq places Bilal's adhan on the Ka'ba on the day of the conquest; 49:13 grounds rank in conduct, not lineage.
